Serlie Barroga-Jamias has advised 15 theses in this repository between 2019 and 2026. Their supervision covers a wide range of subjects, with a primary focus on communication studies, which accounts for 9 items. Other significant research areas include culture and identity (5), arts and creative practice (4), and public health and COVID-19 (4). Additionally, they have supervised work related to social media (2), community development (1), journalism and news media (1), artificial intelligence (1), youth and family (1), and gender and inclusion (1). Their research interests appear to span various methodologies, including phenomenology, autoethnography, quantitative surveys, and qualitative focus group discussions.

The breadth of their supervision is evident in the diverse topics they have overseen. In the realm of communication studies, they have advised work on Filipino virtual assistants as global practitioners, the role of chatbots in government digital transformation, and the use of music as a communicative phenomenon. Their involvement in culture and identity is reflected in studies regarding third culture kids, sexual orientation microaggressions in the workplace, and the intersection of spirituality and social transformation. Regarding public health and COVID-19, they have supervised research on the lived experiences of community journalists, media literacy in relation to misinformation among graduate students, and the role of social media users as gatekeepers of information during the pandemic. Their supervision also extends to arts and creative practice, including research on musical composition and digital advocacy movements.

The most recent thesis advised in this repository is from 2026, which focuses on the lived experiences of Filipino virtual assistants. Their supervision patterns show a consistent engagement with contemporary social issues, such as digital transformation, social media dynamics, and the impact of global events like the COVID-19 pandemic on different sectors of society. While they have a significant number of supervised theses, they have no authored articles currently listed in this repository. Their research focus shows a strong connection to the Philippine context, with specific studies located in the Cordillera Administrative Region, Laurel, Batangas, Capas, Tarlac, Guinobatan, Albay, and Davao City. They have also supervised work involving international contexts, such as Filipino migrants in Bangkok, Thailand, and research related to Cambodia. The diversity of their advised topics suggests they are able to supervise students working across various disciplines, including governance, business, and social sciences, provided the core focus remains on communication and its societal implications.
